cim: AI and the Promise of Organized Knowledge
kihagyva: P3: 41 pont, tendencia 20%, jóváhagyás után fordul
cim_eredeti: AI and the Promise of Organized Knowledge
szoveg_eredeti:
Institutions that seek certainty from artificial intelligence risk losing the habits of self-correction and accountability that have made them resilient.

An emergency physician who is struggling to understand a patient’s deteriorating lab results asks an artificial intelligence system for help. The answer arrives in a definitive form, with seeming fluency and confidence. Where a human doctor, faced with the same numbers, might admit uncertainty, order more tests, and proceed with caution, clinical AI tools do not reliably communicate whether a question exceeds their competence or whether the evidence underlying their recommendations is sufficient. Even when excellent data are available, weakly supported and strongly supported answers can be delivered in the same authoritative form. Clinicians are expected to acknowledge the limits of their knowledge in their quest to “do no harm.” An AI given similar authority may fail to make that boundary equally visible.

In Louisiana, a prisoner can lose the opportunity for a parole hearing because of a risk score determined by the TIGER system, an algorithmic model for predicting recidivism developed to guide correctional interventions. Under a 2024 change in the law, only those with a low TIGER risk score can go before the parole board; everyone with a moderate or high score is automatically disqualified. However, the score relies heavily on pre-incarceration characteristics and does not credit subsequent rehabilitation efforts. ProPublica and Verite News documented multiple cases of prisoners whose hearings were canceled on this basis. Among them was a nearly blind 70-year-old man in a wheelchair who had taken anger management classes, learned a trade, and enrolled in drug treatment. He was deemed ineligible for parole because TIGER judged him a moderate risk of reoffending. The problem with TIGER is not only its predictive accuracy; it’s that the score it generates was designed to guide rehabilitation programming—not to assess suitability for parole. Even so, it has been given authority to foreclose institutional judgment on prisoners.

In scientific publishing, the start-up QED Science developed an AI system to assess the originality and validity of life-science manuscripts before publication. In November 2025, the major preprint service bioRxiv launched a pilot integration with QED Science that lets authors send papers directly to the service for AI review. This may be useful quality control. It also raises a key question: Is an assessment of the relation between claims, evidence, and other papers sufficient to determine whether an inquiry is original? And what if it is not papers that need examination but the standards of a field itself? Is AI the kind of peer that can carry out that sort of review?

These cases differ in consequences and technological details, but they share a pattern. Essential institutions, including those we rely on for health care, justice, public policy, and the evaluation of research, are increasingly delegating judgment, in whole or in part, to automated systems. And the outputs of these systems can acquire authority more quickly than the tools needed to scrutinize them can be created.

In transferring judgment to algorithms, these institutions aggressively pursue one of the foundational visions of Enlightenment and post-Enlightenment science. From philosopher Francis Bacon’s novel New Atlantis to science administrator Vannevar Bush’s 1945 report Science, the Endless Frontier, modern societies, even those arrayed along very different cultural and political lines, have presumed that knowledge is what I call organized promise—that scientific and technical power, properly institutionalized, secures collective progress. A key element of this promise is progress toward certainty: the reduction of error, ambiguity, and dispute.

Artificial intelligence inherits and intensifies this promissory tradition. By generating immediate, confident answers, AI offers the impression that uncertainty itself can be managed away. Yet many of the uncertainties inherent in AI—as well as those surrounding climate, pandemics, financial systems, and biotechnology—are permanent features of complex societies.

This is one of the insights of post-normal science (PNS), which fellow philosopher of science Jerry Ravetz and I described decades ago: PNS is not a method but a name for the class of problems in which closure is not available. We showed that where facts are uncertain, values in dispute, stakes high, and decisions urgent, knowledge relevant to public decisions cannot be judged solely through disciplinary or professional expertise—much less through computational pattern matching and conformity with existing knowledge. Quality, in that setting, means fitness for the purpose at hand, and it depends not only on method but on the arrangements through which claims are scrutinized and the institutions offering them are made accountable. Accountability provides the grounds on which knowledge claims acquire authority. Institutions that mistake the appearance of certainty for authority risk losing the habits of self-correction and accountability that make them resilient.

Artificial intelligence is commonly treated as a technological breakthrough, a source of economic disruption, or an existential threat. Those descriptions obscure the institutional form it already takes. AI, as it is presently constituted, is a diverse set of computational architectures and applications that is transforming the social conditions under which knowledge is assessed and governed.

Institutions, including those we rely on for health care, justice, public policy, and the evaluation of research, are increasingly delegating judgment to automated systems.

Many of AI’s most important institutional implications are already here. Automated systems will continue to develop, but the arrangements by which institutions decide what to rely on have changed within a few years, without a defined process, expert mandate, or democratic consultation. PNS helps identify how policymakers and institutional leaders might protect or build those capacities and how institutional resilience might be strengthened.

Trustworthy institutional authority depends on accountability. Human knowledge, however imperfect, can be made accountable because a claimant can be identified, questioned about evidence and reasons, challenged by others, and held answerable for judgment. A large language model (LLM), one prominent form of AI today, stands in a different relation to accountability. An output may have identifiable sources and a recorded prompt, yet the system is not an author in the institutional sense. It cannot be questioned as a responsible claimant or held answerable for the consequences of a judgment. These unaccountable systems are increasingly used to draft reports, summarize research, navigate vast bodies of information, and support professional decisionmaking.

To be sure, the challenge of establishing trustworthy knowledge under conditions of uncertainty predates AI. It arises because evidence is incomplete, experts disagree, values conflict, and decisions cannot wait. Traditional scientific procedures have never been sufficient on their own. Better facts cannot entirely resolve these conditions. Yet governments, corporations, and other organizations adopting knowledge automation routinely treat AI output as the fulfillment of Leibniz’s dream of a calculus ratiocinator, a means of resolving disputes through calculation and abstract reasoning. Today’s AI systems carry this dream into domains once thought resistant to formalization, such as language and social decisionmaking.
